title: After 2 decades, Jamia Millia Islamia announces resumption of student union elections
summary: Jamia Millia Islamia has ordered the holding of students' union elections within 15 days after constitutional approval. The university revoked disciplinary actions taken against students during recent protests and issued an inquiry into security conduct. Protesting students will publicly apologize for statements made against the administration and remove related social media posts. Classes will be conducted online amid the current tensions on campus.
full_text:
Jamia Millia Islamia has ordered the holding of students' union elections within 15 days after constitutional approval.

NEW DELHI: Jamia Millia Islamia has ordered the resumption of students’ union elections, stating that polls will be held within 15 days of approval of the union’s constitution. The university has also revoked suspension orders and show-cause notices issued to students during the ongoing protest and announced an inquiry into the conduct of security personnel during the agitation. However, protesting students have rejected the administration’s order, calling it ambiguous and insisting that the agitation will continue until their demands are addressed through clear, written commitments. An order issued by Registrar Md Mahtab Alam Rizvi on Monday, October 26, states that elections to the Jamia Millia Islamia Students’ Union (JMISU) will be held 15 days after the union’s constitution is approved. It also provides for a committee to inquire into the actions of security staff during the protest. The order came after the administration held talks with students who had submitted a list of demands, including the restoration of the elected students’ union, withdrawal of disciplinary action and an inquiry into alleged excesses by security personnel. According to the order, the protesting students have agreed to issue a public apology through a press conference for allegedly defamatory statements, actions or social media posts targeting the university administration during the agitation. The posts are to be taken down from social media platforms with immediate effect. The order states that the protest will be called off immediately following its issuance. However, the Jammu & Kashmir Students Association said the order did not provide a definite timeline for approval of the union’s constitution or address the students’ demand for the resignation of the proctor. “Assurances without concrete decisions and a clear roadmap cannot be treated as fulfilment of our demands,” the student organisation said in a statement, adding that the agitation would continue until the administration provided written commitments addressing their concerns. According to the association, Registrar Rizvi arrived on campus around 4.30am on Monday for talks with the protesters. He shared the administration’s order and urged the students to end their agitation, saying their demands had been met. The protest has centred on the demand for the restoration of JMISU, whose elections have not been held since 2006. Four students had been on an indefinite hunger strike, while other protesters sought a time-bound election schedule, withdrawal of disciplinary action and an inquiry into the conduct of security personnel. Amid escalating tensions, the university had earlier shifted classes across courses to online mode and advised students against visiting the campus. It had also announced that gates and libraries would remain closed until further notice. The administration had said a seven-member committee of professors held multiple rounds of talks with the protesters. A committee to draft the JMISU constitution was notified on October 21. Students, however, had argued that setting up the drafting committee was insufficient without a definite election timeline and student representation in the process. The latest order addresses some of their demands, including the withdrawal of disciplinary action and an inquiry into the conduct of security personnel. However, the lack of a fixed deadline for approval of the constitution remains a key point of contention. (With agency inputs)

End of Article

title: Concerns about quality of health care, unemployment, as RMPs in Keralam cross one-lakh mark
summary: As many as 31,446 doctors got their registrations between 2021 and 2025, show data from the Kerala State Medical Councils
full_text:
The number of registered medical practitioners (RMP) in Keralam has crossed one-lakh mark, and 32.75% of them got their registrations between 2021 and 2025, data collected from the Kerala State Medical Councils (KSMC) till October 8, 2026, show.

According to RTI data collected from the KSMC, there are 1,13,023 RMPs in the State. As many as 31,446 doctors were registered between 2021 and 2025. A total of 5,981 doctors got registered in 2021, 5,734 in 2022, 5,283 in 2023, 7,065 in 2024, and 7,383 in 2025. As many as 2,695 doctors registered with the KSMC till October 8 this year.

K.V. Babu, Kannur-based ophthalmologist and public health activist, who gathered the information, says that 95,993 doctors were added to the list in the last 27 years. “Keralam’s population is around 3.62 crore. Among the above-mentioned doctors, at least some may have migrated to other States or abroad seeking better opportunities. However, if at least 80,000 of them are here, there is one MBBS doctor for a population of 450 people already,” he says. Dr. Babu claims that the consequences of this trend could be unemployment among medical graduates and commercialisation of health care.

Seats fall vacant

“According to reports, hundreds of MBBS seats have fallen vacant in [deemed-to-be universities] in Tamil Nadu this year [after the final round of counselling for the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test for undergraduate medical courses]. A similar phenomenon could happen in Keralam as well. The government should study this issue before giving permission for new medical colleges,” he says.

M.N. Menon, president, Indian Medical Association (IMA), Kerala State branch, says around 5,000 graduates are coming out of medical colleges in the State every year. “Another 2,000 are passing out from other States and countries. Unemployment among new medical graduates is already high. Instead of granting sanction for new medical colleges, the government should improve the infrastructure in the existing ones and deploy qualified faculty members. Also, we are seeing shortage of doctors and faculty members in government hospitals and government medical colleges. The focus should also be on appointing necessary staff there,” Dr. Menon adds.

title: Political Line | Local, national, and anti-national
summary: Here is the latest edition of the Political Line newsletter curated by Varghese K. George
full_text:
To be, or not to be — like Kerala

This week, the entire newsletter is around questions related to federalism - Centre-State relations and the organising principles of India as a nation. So I am not marking out a separate Federalism Tract segment.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi responded to Congress Rahul Gandhi’s speech on federalism and diversity by terming it separatist and divisive ; Mr. Modi also said the Congress party was taken over by ‘urban Naxals.’

BJP Chief Minister in Uttar Pradesh Yogi Adityanath warned voters in the State that it might turn into another Kashmir, Kerala or West Bengal. That would be better for the people of U.P., Kerala CM Pinarayi Vijayan, West Bengal CM Mamata Banerjee and former CM of Jammu and Kashmir Omar Abdullah retorted, in their own individual styles. These three fare far better than U.P. in all human development indices in the Niti Aayog country-wide ranking. What is common between these two States and a Union Territory that caught the attention of the U.P. CM? One does not know. Kerala, West Bengal and Jammu and Kashmir have the highest proportion of Muslims in the country, and they enjoy proportionate political power.

Jobs for locals

The Haryana government has moved the Supreme Court to restore a State law that reserves 75% private jobs up to a particular level to domiciles, after the High Court stayed it . The State has a BJP-led coalition government, and the party publicly stands for a ‘One Nation’ policy. Haryana is not the first State to have enacted laws that reserve jobs for locals. Such laws challenge the conception of India as a nation — where citizens have constitutionally guaranteed rights that are restricted according to domicile only in rare cases. This piece discusses the constitutional questions arising out of Haryana’s nativist politics. This article also points out that for reservations, same considerations may not be equally applicable in education and employment.

Meanwhile, the Haryana government is moving towards a new law to restrict religious conversions .

NEET closure? Not quite

Tamil Nadu’s attempts to restore its powers in admissions to medical schools in the State are continuing, in the face of resistance from the Governor. The State Assembly has passed the NEET Exemption Bill to reclaim its powers for a second time, after it was returned by the Governor. The national admission policy goes against the spirit of federalism and social justice, Chief Minister M.K. Stalin told the State Assembly. He also said the Tamil Nadu’s Legislature’s sovereignty and rights must be preserved. A succinct backgrounder and the State’s arguments can be found here , in Mr. Stalin’s own words.

Now that the law has been passed again, what can or will the Governor do? Is this going to be a conflict between the Centre and Tamil Nadu? Constitutionally, the President has the power to hold back the Bill or not deny assent. The role of the Governor and the President in this process is explained in this piece .

For a wider discussion on the role of Governors and their relationship with Chief Ministers, read this .

Delimitation in Jammu and Kashmir

The process of redrawing the political map of Jammu and Kashmir is underway. Regional parties in the Union Territory fear that the proposed electoral map of the UT is aimed at reducing the political clout of Muslims in the Valley.

According to the draft report, the Valley that has 56% of the population gets 52% of the seats in the Assembly (47 of 90 seats); the Jammu region that has 44% of the population gets 47% of the seats. This has been justified on the grounds such as remoteness of a place. You can find more details in this explainer .

Language questions

A DMK member demanded in the Lok Sabha that answers to questions asked in English must be in English.

A stealth invasion of Hindi into slots occupied by Malayalam programmes from All India Radio’s Thiruvananthapuram station has resulted in protests.

title: The Art of Storytelling to Engage Students
summary:

The post The Art of Storytelling to Engage Students appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
Have you ever connected your lesson with your students to a personal experience or a story you witnessed? If not, you should. Watch the engagement in the students’ eyes as they lean into the story you are telling. The students will want to hear more, asking questions and encouraging you to give more details. Students want to learn, but even more than that, they want to connect with the material they consume.

Storytelling as a Tool for Critical Thinking

Storytelling is a humanizing practice that can guide inquiry and foster critical thinking (Nagarkar et al., 2026; Astiz, 2020). Critical thinking is a skill that many students struggle to develop. Sometimes, it is easy to get a student to agree with you, but very difficult to teach them to think critically on their own (Bowen & Watson, 2018). Some of our students want the answer or have us teach to the test. However, especially in healthcare fields, critical thinking and learning the material beyond exams are important.

I have found that when I connect the concept to a story, the students are engaged and more permeable. The questions asked are mostly a desire to hear the nitty-gritty of the experience, but through that, you will be able to connect the story to your teaching material. I promise you, they will remember the material more deeply than if you spoon-fed it to them. The idea is that the student can later reflect on that story to remember not only the details but also the material being taught, connecting the lesson.

You are supporting your students’ learning through storytelling that allows for experiences and truths some will choose not to tell, or that change the narratives told (Astiz, 2020).

Using Personal Experiences to Teach Real-World Lessons

An example of how storytelling can teach a lesson is in reviewing patients’ medical histories.

I was seeing a patient in a dental office for a routine appointment. I examined the patient’s medical history and found nothing concerning, so I asked the standard follow-up question: “Has anything changed in your medical history in the last six months?”

The patient happily replied, “No changes.” So, I began the dental cleaning. I did not get far when I noticed some bandages on my patient’s knee.

“What happened?” I asked. “Did you fall?”

“No,” they replied. “I had my knee replaced.”

I immediately stopped because, several years ago, the protocol for dental prophylaxis for knee replacement was antibiotic premedication. I was horrified at my inability to take a full history on the patient and at having begun treatment when the protocol was that they could not get their teeth cleaned without the premedication. Had I taken a few extra minutes and asked more detailed questions, the patient likely would have responded appropriately by noting that they had a surgical procedure.

Storytelling has been used for centuries by many cultures to convey health-related knowledge (Nagarkar et al., 2026). Findings from a recent scoping review emphasized that storytelling is not only a promising modality for enhancing health knowledge but also a culturally grounded approach to advancing health equity (Nagarkar et al., 2026).

I used this humbling experience not only to provide a real-world example that could teach students important lessons but also to enhance their knowledge of health.

Connecting the Story to the Lesson

So, what is the lesson here? What I want the students to take from this story is multifunctional.

First, it is important to acknowledge that everyone makes mistakes, even teachers. Second, a detailed medical history can prevent medical errors. Third, there are situations in which merely posing the question does not give a patient enough background information to provide an accurate response. Finally, think critically about the importance of knowing your patient’s medical history.

How do you know if students comprehended the purpose of the lesson when the story is told? Start a discussion. Ask your students why they think the story was important. How did it connect to the day’s lesson? Initiate a conversation where you can summarize the lesson’s main ideas and make sure everyone understands.

Therefore, the next time you want to teach a new lesson—or even one you have been teaching for some time—consider incorporating a creative plot or personal experience to help relate the content to practical applications.

Tiffany Baggs, CRDH, MSDH, is a Professor for the Dental Hygiene program at Valencia College. She is an active member of the Florida Dental Hygiene Association (FDHA) and the Florida Allied Dental Educators Association (FADE).

References

Astiz, M. F. 2020. “Storytelling in the Higher Education Classroom: Why It Matters.” College Teaching 68 (4): 187–188. https://doi.org/10.1080/87567555.2020.1785382

Bowen, J. A., and C. E. Watson. 2018. Teaching Naked Techniques: A Practical Guide to Designing Better Classes. 1st ed. Hoboken, NJ: Jossey-Bass.

title: Freiheit im Netz auf Talfahrt: Zensur, KI, Alterschecks und digitale Isolation
summary: Der Freedom-on-the-Net-Bericht 2026 verweist auf weltweit sinkende Internetfreiheiten. Autokraten isolieren Netze; Altersgrenzen und KI schaffen neue Hürden.
full_text:
close notice

This article is also available in English. It was translated with technical assistance and editorially reviewed before publication.

.

Die Freiheit im Internet befindet sich weltweit weiter im Sinkflug. Laut einem neuen Bericht der US-Organisation Freedom House verzeichnete sie bereits im 16. Jahr in Folge einen globalen Rückgang. In der am Freitag veröffentlichten Studie „Freedom on the Net 2026“ verschlechterten sich die Bedingungen in 16 der 38 untersuchten Staaten. Nur in acht Ländern machten die Experten Verbesserungen aus.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Zu den Schlusslichtern zählen unverändert China und Myanmar. Im Iran erlebte die Online-Freiheit den drastischsten Einbruch. Nach der gewaltsamen Niederschlagung von Protesten und militärischen Auseinandersetzungen verhängten die Behörden eine rund 88-tägige Internetsperre – die längste in der Weltgeschichte. Zugleich strukturierten sie das Netz so um, heißt es, dass nur noch eine privilegierte Elite Zugang zum globalen Internet erhalte. Die breite Bevölkerung werde systematisch ausgesperrt.

Autoritäre Regime verfeinern laut den Autoren ihre Strategien zur digitalen Isolation. In Russland treibe Präsident Wladimir Putin die Kontrolle über Internetprovider voran, um den Zugang auf staatlich genehmigte Plattformen zu beschränken und VPNs zu behindern. Ähnliche Tendenzen zeigten sich in Kirgisistan, wo der staatliche Einfluss auf den internationalen Datenverkehr deutlich ausgebaut worden sei. Diktatoren investierten gezielt in die Trennung ihrer Gesellschaften vom weltweiten Informationsfluss. Umso wichtiger blieben zensurresistente Technologien und Umgehungswerkzeuge wie das Anonymisierungsnetzwerk Tor für Aktivisten und Journalisten.

Altersprüfung als neues Überwachungsrisiko

Neben staatlicher Zensur breiteten sich weltweit Gesetze zur Altersverifikation aus, moniert die NGO. Unter dem Deckmantel des Jugendschutzes ermöglichten sie erhebliche Eingriffe in die Privatsphäre. Nach dem Inkrafttreten des weltweit ersten Verbots sozialer Medien für unter 16-Jährige in Australien Ende 2025 hätten weitere Staaten Altersgrenzen eingeführt oder vorgeschlagen.

Die Maßnahmen erforderten häufig die Verarbeitung sensibler Daten wie Gesichtsscans oder amtlicher Ausweise, beklagen die Verfasser. Das schaffe Einfallstore für Überwachung und erhebliche Cybersicherheitsrisiken, wie Datenlecks bei Drittanbietern zeigten. In Ländern wie der Türkei drohe zudem die Verknüpfung von Social-Media-Konten mit staatlichen Identitätssystemen. Oppositionelle und Dissidenten würden dadurch noch gläserner.

Auch Künstliche Intelligenz verändert die digitale Landschaft grundlegend. Regierungen versuchten zwar zunehmend, Deepfakes, nicht einvernehmliche intime Bilder und Online-Belästigung einzudämmen. In den USA trat dazu der Take It Down Act in Kraft. In Indien und Mexiko führten strenge Kennzeichnungspflichten für synthetische Inhalte und Gesetze gegen Identitätsmissbrauch dagegen zu kurzen Löschfristen und willkürlichen Verhaftungen von Online-Journalisten. Autokratische Akteure instrumentalisieren KI zunehmend zur Kontrolle und Unterdrückung von Meinungen, statt freie Diskurse zu schützen.

Auch Demokratien sind nicht gefeit

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Selbst gefestigte Demokratien stehen laut der Analyse unter Druck. Die USA stagnieren mit 73 von 100 möglichen Punkten auf einem recht niedrigen Niveau der Internetfreiheit. Anhaltende Überwachung, behördlicher Druck auf Online-Aktivisten und schärfere juristische Strafen für digitale Meinungsäußerungen belasteten die Grundrechte.

Deutschland, das in früheren Auswertungen mit mehr als 85 Punkten zu den freiheitlichsten Online-Umgebungen gehörte, ist wegen einer veränderten Methodik und der Konzentration auf 38 ausgewählte Schwerpunktnationen in der aktuellen Ausgabe nicht mehr direkt im globalen Vergleich vertreten. Europäische Debatten über Altersverifikation, Upload-Filter, Verschlüsselung und Plattformregulierung spiegeln aber auch hierzulande den Konflikt zwischen Schutzmaßnahmen und der Wahrung von Privatsphäre und Meinungsfreiheit wider. Im Vorjahr hatte Deutschland drei Punkte verloren.

Angesichts dieser Entwicklungen fordert Freedom House, Demokratien müssten entschlossen handeln und massiv in zensurresistente Werkzeuge, Satelliteninternet und robuste digitale Sicherheitsvorkehrungen investieren. Nur durch internationale Kooperation und den Schutz grundlegender digitaler Rechte lasse sich verhindern, dass das Internet endgültig zum Instrument staatlicher Totalüberwachung werde. Die NGO erhält einen Großteil ihrer Mittel vom US-Außenministerium. Diese Zuschüsse sollen allerdings nicht für die Erstellung des Berichts verwendet werden.
